content:
We can be sure that Apple will raise prices when it unveils the iPhone 18 Pro next month. When Apple raised prices across the board due to rising memory costs, it didn't raise prices on the existing iPhone lineup at the same time, but that was only a temporary reprieve.

However, two sources now say the Pro model's starting price this year will be $1,399—and I can hardly believe even Apple would go that far...

Don't get me wrong: Apple has made it very clear that it wants to protect its profit margins, and it has never shied away from raising prices significantly. For example, the base-model MacBook Air went from $1,099 to $1,299, a $200 increase. Even the MacBook Neo, which initially surprised with its $599 starting price, has gone up by $100.

But a $300 increase in the starting price of the iPhone Pro is just ridiculous. That's the kind of increase Apple has so far reserved for products that cost a lot more.

Among products with $300 price hikes, the cheapest is the base-model MacBook Pro, which went from $1,699 to $1,999. That increase is indeed substantial, just under 18%. But a $300 premium over the previous generation for the iPhone 18 Pro works out to a 27% price hike.

Most Liked Comment from IndomitableSlake

They'll charge whatever they want, and customers will pay it. The housing, auto, and appliance industries have already proven that. Why would this be any different? They'll just take out a loan. 120 years of social and economic history has proven there are absolutely no consequences to long-term debt; might as well take out another loan.

Again, this price increase is not entirely impossible. For example, some MacBook configuration upgrades have literally doubled in price; Apple loves to make profits. But Tim Cook did hint on an earnings call that the company doesn't want to protect its profit margins at all costs.

As for sales, I do think this price hike will put a lot of people off upgrading, especially since it looks like next year's Pro model will be a more significant upgrade.

Of course, the counterargument is that the Apple Upgrade program can ease some of the pressure. People may feel it's fine to rent an iPhone 18 Pro for a year and then upgrade to the 20th anniversary model next year. But for those buying outright, a price hike of this magnitude will be a significant deterrent.

What do you think? Do you think a $300 increase is reasonable, or is a 27% hike too much even for Apple? Feel free to share your views in the comments.
